newsitem.title: JAPAN: APEC finance ministers to forge standards in Cebu.
newsitem.headline: APEC finance ministers to forge standards in Cebu.

text.p: Asia-Pacific finance ministers make a start this weekend on the Herculean task of trying to forge common standards for financial markets among the region's wildly diverse economies.
"I don't think it will be easy to draw a consensus," said Choi Joong-kyung, South Korean Finance Ministry director of financial policy and international relations.
"But the direction has been agreed upon -- deregulation, liberalisation and transparency."

The first step down the new and rocky road starts when the Finance ministers of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meet in the Philippine island resort of Cebu on Saturday and Sunday, their fourth gathering since an inaugural meeting in March 1994 in Honolulu, Hawaii.

The finance ministers have been charged by the leaders of APEC -- nations with vast differences in culture and in economy -- with coming up with concrete measures to match a vision of a Pacific Rim free trade zone of half the world's population.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.

Japanese officials said the group hoped to get "visible and concrete" proposals from each member to make regulations more stable and transparent, lure more investment into the region and promote freer flow of capital.
Previous meetings discussed the issues in principle, but "now they want to get officials to really talk about a plan of action," a senior Malaysian finance official said.
But there are signs of a rift forming within the diverse group, even before the ministers get to the table.
An Indonesian finance ministry official said the developed countries, especially Japan and Singapore, were very keen for proposals promoting financial and capital market development.
"They want to liberalise it as fast as possible. They want things like cross-listing. But we are not ready yet," he said.
South Korea's Choi agreed.
"Some countries are reluctant to go for full-fledged liberalisation based on the experience of Chile and Mexico. Each country is in a different stage of development."

The more affluent of the pack have gone ahead and formed their own economic clique -- dubbed the "G6" or the Group of Six, likening it to the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations which meets regularly to coordinate economic policy.

The G6 -- comprised of senior financial and central bank officials from Australia, China, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore and the United State -- met in Tokyo in March, but the purpose was mainly to bring China into the grouping.

Australian analysts said APEC differed from other trade groupings such as the European Union (EU) or the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), because there was greater diversity in terms of economic development.
They said APEC's consensus approach, as opposed to the more formal, legally-binding structure used in groups such as the EU, made objectives harder to achieve quickly.

"In APEC, I think they are extremely worthy goals, but they are medium to long term and they're just not going to have much impact on markets in the short term," Commonwealth Bank of Australia chief economist Bruce Freeland said.
Proposals to create stable and transparent regulations should help to attract investment into the region to foot the bill to develop Asian infrastructure, a Japanese official said.
"No private company would risk investing in a country where clear and stable regulations do not exist," the official said.
By some estimates, the region needs $2 trillion worth of infrastructure development in the next decade and private investment is crucial for this, he added.
"Whether ministers say it or not, Asia's financial markets will catch up with America and Europe. It's just a matter of time," a senior treasury official at a Philippine bank said.
